explanations.explanation: Livestock is it, baker. These two tribes had very large herds and flocks, and they saw that Jazer and Gilead were suitable for livestock (Numbers 32:1). When you own that many animals, you look at a field and see a dinner table. I do the same thing with a counter and a cooling rack.

Vineyards are a nice thought, but the text never brings them up. The verse says they surveyed Jazer and Gilead and saw the region was suitable for livestock. These tribes had very large herds and flocks, so the grass was what caught their eyes. No grapes in this chapter.

Trade makes sense as a guess, but it isn't in the verse. The text says the Reubenites and Gadites had very large herds and flocks, and they saw the land was suitable for livestock. Nobody is setting up a market stand here. They're looking at pasture.

explanations.answer: Let them have this land and not cross
explanations.explanation: That's the ask. They say, “…let this land be given to your servants as a possession. Do not make us cross the Jordan.” (Numbers 32:5). Nice and polite on the front, and then the big request lands. I think I'd be a little nervous too if I was sitting across from Moses, Israel's leader, with that one.

explanations.answer: Let them have more of the war spoil
explanations.explanation: War spoil never comes up in their request. They ask for this land, the east side, as a possession, and they ask not to cross the Jordan (Numbers 32:5). The whole pitch is about where they'll settle. It's one ask, and it's about land.

explanations.answer: Let them take the best land in Canaan
explanations.explanation: They're actually asking to stay out of Canaan. They want the land they're standing in, and they say, “Do not make us cross the Jordan.” (Numbers 32:5). So the best land across the river isn't what they're after. They've picked their spot already.

Not quite, baker. Moses doesn't say yes at all. He answers with a question: “Shall your brothers go to war while you sit here?” (Numbers 32:6). He starts with a hard question before he says anything else.

False is right. Moses doesn't say yes, and he doesn't even say no yet. He asks, “Shall your brothers go to war while you sit here?” (Numbers 32:6). When a leader answers your big ask with a question, you know you're about to have a long talk.

That's what he says. Moses asks, “Why are you discouraging the Israelites from crossing into the land that the LORD has given them?” (Numbers 32:7). Notice he doesn't say they said anything. He's talking about what their plan would do to everybody else.

explanations.answer: Taking the best pasture for themselves
explanations.explanation: Pasture isn't what Moses brings up. His question is, “Why are you discouraging the Israelites from crossing into the land that the LORD has given them?” (Numbers 32:7). He's worried about what this does to the rest of Israel crossing over. The second question is about crossing, not about grass.

Egypt isn't in his question. Moses says they're discouraging the Israelites from crossing into the land the LORD has given them (Numbers 32:7). The problem he names is about going forward into the land. That's the whole second question.

Their fathers, yes. Moses says, “This is what your fathers did when I sent them from Kadesh-barnea to inspect the land.” (Numbers 32:8). He's pulling an old family story out of the closet. I bet nobody in that room wanted that one on the table.

The Moabites don't show up in Moses' words here. He points straight at the fathers of these Reubenites and Gadites, the ones he sent from Kadesh-barnea to inspect the land (Numbers 32:8). He's talking about their own family history. Nobody from outside gets blamed.

Egypt isn't who Moses names. He says, “This is what your fathers did when I sent them from Kadesh-barnea to inspect the land.” (Numbers 32:8). The ones who discouraged Israel were their own fathers. That's why the comparison hits so close to home.

True. Moses says, “So the anger of the LORD was kindled that day, and He swore an oath…” (Numbers 32:10). The fathers discouraged Israel from entering the land the LORD had given them, and the oath followed. That's why Moses is bringing it up now.

It's actually true, baker. Moses says, “So the anger of the LORD was kindled that day, and He swore an oath…” (Numbers 32:10). That came after their fathers discouraged the Israelites from entering the land. The oath is what Moses spells out in the next verses.

Twenty or older, that's the line. The LORD says not one of the men twenty years of age or older who came out of Egypt will see the land (Numbers 32:11). Moses says it was because they did not follow Him wholeheartedly. The oath came with a clear age line.

Thirty is close to the ballpark, but the number is twenty. The oath covers “…not one of the men twenty years of age or older who came out of Egypt…” (Numbers 32:11). So the line is drawn a decade lower than thirty. That makes the group bigger than you'd think.

Fifty is way past the line. The LORD says it's the men twenty years of age or older who came out of Egypt (Numbers 32:11). That takes in a whole lot more men than fifty and up would. The text names twenty.

Caleb is right. The LORD names “Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite” as one exception (Numbers 32:12). The reason given is that he did follow the LORD wholeheartedly. Out of that whole generation, he made the short list.

Joshua is right. He's “Joshua son of Nun,” the other exception in the oath (Numbers 32:12). The LORD says they did follow Him wholeheartedly. Moses is going to hand him orders later in this same chapter.
Aaron, Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), isn't named in this oath. The two exceptions are Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun (Numbers 32:12). He doesn't even show up in this chapter.

Eleazar the priest is in this chapter. Moses is talking to him with the leaders in Numbers 32:2. But the oath's two exceptions are Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun (Numbers 32:12). Eleazar's just in the room.

Phinehas, Eleazar's son (Numbers 25:7), isn't anywhere in this passage. The oath names Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun as the two exceptions (Numbers 32:12). He didn't even get a cameo. Nice name, though.

Forty years. The text says He “made them wander in the wilderness forty years, until the whole generation who had done evil in His sight was gone.” (Numbers 32:13). That's a lot of walking. I thought my years in a drawer were long.

Twelve is a lot shorter than what the text says. It's forty years of wandering in the wilderness, until that whole generation was gone (Numbers 32:13). The number is bigger than most people want to wait.

Seven is far from it, baker. Moses says the LORD made them wander in the wilderness forty years (Numbers 32:13). It lasted until the whole generation who had done evil in His sight was gone. Forty is the number.

Wilderness is it. Moses warns that if they turn away from following Him, “He will once again leave this people in the wilderness…” (Numbers 32:15). That word 'again' is doing a lot of work. Moses is reminding them where that road leads.

A valley does show up in this talk, the Valley of Eshcol in verse 9, but not here. The warning in verse 15 says He will once again leave this people in the wilderness. That's the place Moses points back to. The word is wilderness.

Hills aren't in Moses' warning. He says that if they turn away from following Him, the LORD “will once again leave this people in the wilderness” (Numbers 32:15). The place he names is the wilderness. He's pointing at the forty years from earlier.
Arm is the word. They say, “But we will arm ourselves and be ready to go ahead of the Israelites…” (Numbers 32:17). That's the piece that changes the whole deal. They're not just staying put anymore.

Number is a clever guess, but the verse says something different. They say, “But we will arm ourselves and be ready to go ahead of the Israelites…” (Numbers 32:17). It's about getting armed and going out front. Counting isn't part of this deal.

Humble sounds nice, but that's not the word. Their men say they will arm themselves and be ready to go ahead of the Israelites (Numbers 32:17). This part of the plan is about going into battle first. It's a very practical promise.

True. They say, “We will not return to our homes until every Israelite has taken possession of his inheritance.” (Numbers 32:18). That's a big promise, and it covers every Israelite. The little ones stay behind in the fortified cities while the men go.

It's actually true, baker. They say, “We will not return to our homes until every Israelite has taken possession of his inheritance.” (Numbers 32:18). They commit to stay until every Israelite has his inheritance. That's the heart of their new plan.

explanations.answer: They may go home and the land is theirs
explanations.explanation: That's the deal. Moses says that when the land is subdued before the LORD, “you may return and be free of obligation to the LORD and to Israel. And this land will belong to you as a possession before the LORD.” (Numbers 32:22). Work first, then home. Not bad for a promise that started with a lot of questions.

explanations.answer: They get first pick of land in Canaan
explanations.explanation: They already said they won't take an inheritance across the Jordan (Numbers 32:19). So first pick of Canaan isn't on the table. Moses says they may return, and the land they asked for will belong to them as a possession (Numbers 32:22). Their reward is the land they picked.

explanations.answer: They get to lead every tribe in battle
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't hand out any leadership role here. He says that once the land is subdued, they may return and the land will be theirs (Numbers 32:22). Their promise was to go ahead of the Israelites, and the reward is simply going home. No trophy, just the land.

Moses says the opposite. He tells them, “But if you do not do this, you will certainly sin against the LORD—and be assured that your sin will find you out.” (Numbers 32:23). So it's not something that stays hidden. The words are very plain.

False is right. Moses says, “But if you do not do this, you will certainly sin against the LORD—and be assured that your sin will find you out.” (Numbers 32:23). It's a serious line, so he says it plainly. He wants them to know it before they promise.

That's the add-on. Moses says, “Build cities for your little ones and folds for your flocks, but do what you have promised.” (Numbers 32:24). He gives them the okay and then holds them to their word. Short and simple.

explanations.answer: Pay a tribute to the LORD
explanations.explanation: No tribute is mentioned here. Moses says, “Build cities for your little ones and folds for your flocks, but do what you have promised.” (Numbers 32:24). The one condition is keeping what they already said. That's all he adds.

Moses doesn't give them a building deadline. He says, “Build cities for your little ones and folds for your flocks, but do what you have promised.” (Numbers 32:24). What he cares about is the promise. The cities just get the green light.

explanations.answer: They will do just as Moses commands
explanations.explanation: That's their answer. They say, “Your servants will do just as our lord commands.” (Numbers 32:25). No arguing, no extra bargaining. They agree right there.

explanations.answer: They ask for time to think it over
explanations.explanation: They don't ask for any time. They answer right away: “Your servants will do just as our lord commands.” (Numbers 32:25). There's no pause in the text. They say yes on the spot.

explanations.answer: They offer to send half their men
explanations.explanation: Half isn't what they say. They tell Moses, “…every man will cross over to the battle before the LORD, just as our lord says.” (Numbers 32:27). Every man is the promise. Not a single one stays behind.

explanations.answer: Among the other tribes in Canaan
explanations.explanation: That's the backup rule. Moses says, “But if they do not arm themselves and go across with you, then they must accept their possession among you in the land of Canaan.” (Numbers 32:30). So if they skip the fight, they don't keep the east side. They'd get their land with everyone else.

explanations.answer: In the land of Gilead anyway
explanations.explanation: Gilead only stays theirs if they keep the promise. Moses says, “But if they do not arm themselves and go across with you, then they must accept their possession among you in the land of Canaan.” (Numbers 32:30). So the 'anyway' part isn't in the deal. The land depends on the promise.

The wilderness isn't what Moses names here. He says that if they don't cross armed, “…they must accept their possession among you in the land of Canaan.” (Numbers 32:30). Their land would be in Canaan, among the other tribes. That's the fallback.
LORD is the word. They say, “As the LORD has spoken to your servants, so we will do.” (Numbers 32:31). They're pointing past Moses to the One who spoke. That's a serious thing to promise.

The priest isn't who they name. Eleazar the priest got orders from Moses back in verse 28, but their answer is, “As the LORD has spoken to your servants, so we will do.” (Numbers 32:31). It's the LORD they name. He's the one they're promising in front of.
No council is named in their reply. They say, “As the LORD has spoken to your servants, so we will do.” (Numbers 32:31). The one they point to is the LORD. Their promise is made before Him.

Manasseh is right. Moses gives the land to the Gadites, the Reubenites and “the half-tribe of Manasseh son of Joseph” (Numbers 32:33). So only half of Manasseh settles east of the Jordan. It's a tribe cut in two.

Judah isn't mentioned in this chapter at all. Moses gives the land to the Gadites, the Reubenites and the half-tribe of Manasseh son of Joseph (Numbers 32:33). So Judah isn't in this deal. It's just those three groups.
Levi doesn't appear in this land hand-out. Verse 33 says Moses gave it to the Gadites, the Reubenites and the half-tribe of Manasseh son of Joseph. Those are the three groups. Levi's not on the list.

That's what happens. The text says the descendants of Machir son of Manasseh “went to Gilead, captured it, and drove out the Amorites who were there.” (Numbers 32:39). Machir was Manasseh's son. Gilead was the land those tribes had been eyeing since the start.

Peace isn't what the verse says. It says Machir's descendants went to Gilead, captured it, and “drove out the Amorites who were there.” (Numbers 32:39). So the Amorites leave. That's the whole report.

Nobody gets put to work here. The text says the descendants of Machir son of Manasseh captured Gilead and “drove out the Amorites who were there.” (Numbers 32:39). That's the one action it names. The Amorites are driven out.
True. The text says, “So Moses gave Gilead to the clan of Machir son of Manasseh, and they settled there.” (Numbers 32:40). After the capture, they have a home. Quiet ending to that little story.

It's actually true, baker. The verse says Moses gave Gilead to the clan of Machir son of Manasseh, and they settled there (Numbers 32:40). That follows right after they captured it. So Gilead has new residents.
Not quite. Nobah captured Kenath and its villages, but he didn't keep the name. He “called it Nobah, after his own name.” (Numbers 32:42). He put his own name on the place. The old name got replaced.

False is right. Nobah went and captured Kenath and its villages, and he “called it Nobah, after his own name.” (Numbers 32:42). So Kenath got a brand new name. If I ever get a town, I'm calling it Dorin Heights.
